title: A Small Step Sets Calcium Loss

scenes.tts: Your kidneys filter about ten grams of calcium a day. You lose about a fifth of a gram in urine. So almost all the filtered calcium goes back into the blood. What sets that last small fraction? Work it out with made-up round numbers, for a reference adult at steady state.
scenes.visual: bar of filtered calcium; almost all returns to blood, a thin sliver is lost in urine; question mark on the sliver; three tags for the made-up case
scenes.narration: Your kidneys filter about ten grams of calcium a day. You lose about a fifth of a gram in urine. So almost all the filtered calcium goes back into the blood. What sets that last small fraction? Work it out with made-up round numbers, for a reference adult at steady state.

scenes.tts: In adult plasma, roughly half the calcium is ionized, about forty percent bound to protein, and about ten percent complexed. Calcium bound to protein is not filtered. A G F R of one hundred twenty-five millilitres per minute is one hundred eighty litres a day. Total calcium is one hundred milligrams per litre, and sixty percent is filterable. So the filtered load is ten thousand eight hundred milligrams per day.
scenes.caption: In adult plasma, roughly half the calcium is ionized, about 40 percent bound to protein, and about 10 percent complexed. Calcium bound to protein is not filtered. A GFR of 125 mL/min is 180 L a day. Total calcium is 100 mg/L, and 60 percent is filterable. So the filtered load is 10,800 mg per day.
scenes.visual: plasma calcium bar in three pockets; protein-bound pocket crossed out; filterable bracket; three working lines ending in the filtered load

scenes.tts: Most of that is reabsorbed along the tubule. Roughly sixty to seventy percent of filtered calcium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Twenty to twenty five percent is reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb, largely between cells. The distal convoluted and connecting tubules take back roughly five to ten percent, through cells. Parathyroid hormone, or P T H, fine-tunes this small step and also acts upstream.

scenes.tts: Urinary calcium in the example is two hundred milligrams per day. That is one point eight five percent of the filtered load, so ninety-eight point one five percent is reabsorbed. Now let reabsorption fall to ninety-seven percent, with the same filtered load, as when P T H falls. Excretion becomes three hundred twenty-four milligrams per day, one point six two times the original. A fall of about one point one five percentage points moves excretion by sixty-two percent.
scenes.caption: Urinary calcium in the example is 200 mg per day. That is 1.85 percent of the filtered load, so 98.15 percent is reabsorbed. Now let reabsorption fall to 97 percent, with the same filtered load, as when PTH falls. Excretion becomes 324 mg per day, 1.62 times the original. A fall of about 1.15 percentage points moves excretion by 62 percent.

scenes.tts: The parathyroid chief cells carry the calcium sensing receptor, which reads ionized calcium. A rise in ionized calcium activates the receptor and inhibits P T H secretion. The response is steep: a small change in calcium moves secretion a long way. P T H raises active calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron. So when P T H falls, distal reabsorption falls, and with the same filtered load, urinary calcium rises.

scenes.tts: Keep the rule. The kidney filters about ten grams of calcium a day and reabsorbs about ninety-eight percent. The distal step that P T H regulates handles under a tenth of the load. Yet that step fine-tunes urine calcium, along with filtered load.
